hypothesis.title: The Identity Budget
hypothesis.question: Can composition be made more controllable by explicitly deciding which musical features must survive transformation, which may vary, and which should deliberately break when identity changes?
hypothesis.hypothesis: Musical material has an identity budget: recognizability is not identical to acoustic fidelity, but is carried by selected invariants such as prosody, graph path, contour, stress, timbral signature, or call-response role. Composers can use this by preserving the invariant that matters while spending other layers for variation.
hypothesis.rationaleMd: S2 separates intelligibility from acoustic reconstruction at 200 bps, showing that recognition can be optimized independently from surface fidelity. S4 formalizes semi-fragile identity: a watermark survives benign transformations but breaks under semantics-altering edits. S1 and S6 show prosody-aware alignment and annotation as preservation mechanisms for expressive motion, while S3 suggests harmonic identity can live in graph adjacency/path structure rather than chord labels. S5 gives the studio analogue: the early demo and call-response relation can carry the identity that later polishing may accidentally erase.

recipe.title: Spend the Budget Deliberately
recipe.bodyMd: Build a 60-second call-and-response sketch, then create variants that preserve different invariants. Version A preserves pitch and rhythm while changing timbre. Version B preserves contour and stress while moving pitches through a Tonnetz-adjacent harmonic path. Version C preserves timbre and groove while compressing melodic detail until only the call rhythm remains. Version D embeds a three-accent stress watermark designed to survive reharmonization, resampling, and filtering. Listen blind and mark the point where each version stops feeling like the same phrase. This translates [S2]'s intelligibility/fidelity split, [S4]'s semi-fragile watermarking, [S1]/[S6]'s prosody preservation, [S3]'s graph invariants, and [S5]'s demo-anchor practice into a studio protocol.
dawChecklist: Create a two-bar call phrase and two-bar answer phrase.
Bounce a reference demo before polishing.
Duplicate into four variants: timbre-spend, pitch-spend, detail-compression, stress-watermark.
Keep tempo and macro arrangement constant.
Blind-listen and note where recognizability fails.

protocol.listeningContext: Studio headphones or monitors at safe level, no visual access to DAW arrangement during evaluation.
protocol.listeningMethod: Blind A/B/C/D comparison against the original demo; write down which layer seems to carry identity before revealing variant labels.
